claim: Tau is a microtubule-associated protein required for the formation of synapses.
source: tauMR22 mutant primary neurons at 2 DIV show a decrease in the number of puncta positive for Bruchpilot (Brp) and Synaptotagmin (Syt) (Bruchpilot/Brp: 42%; Synaptotagmin/Syt: 59%; all compared to wildtype control neurons; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced synaptic puncta in tau mutant neurons compared to wildtype controls.

claim: Neuronal expression of UAS-tau-GFP rescues the synapse reduction phenotype in tauMR22 mutant neurons.
source: To confirm that this reduction in synapse numbers was due to the loss of Tau, we performed rescue experiments using Gal4-induced neuronal expression of UAS-tau-GFP (Doerflinger et al., 2003) in tauMR22 mutant neurons. We found a significant improvement of the tauMR22 mutant phenotype (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that re-expression of Tau improves the mutant phenotype.

claim: The spectraplakin Short Stop (Shot) is required for synapse formation.
source: We found a reduction in synapse numbers (Brp: 62%; Syt: 67%; Figure 1C–D), consistent with previous descriptions in vivo (Löhr et al., 2002; Prokop et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced synapse numbers in shot mutant neurons and is consistent with previous published findings.

claim: Neuronal expression of UAS-shot-GFP rescues the synapse reduction phenotype in shot3 mutant neurons.
source: We confirmed that this reduction in synapse numbers was due to the loss of Shot by using Gal4-induced neuronal expression of UAS-shot-GFP (Alves-Silva et al., 2012; Sanchez-Soriano et al., 2009) which significantly rescued the synapse phenotype in shot3 mutant neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), confirming the involvement of Shot.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that re-expression of Shot rescues the mutant phenotype.

claim: Shot and Tau display functional overlap in regulating synapse numbers.
source: In further support of functional overlap, also our genetic interaction studies revealed a synapse reduction phenotype in shot3/+ tauMR22/+ double heterozygous mutant neurons (see later in Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction studies showing synapse reduction in double heterozygous mutants.

claim: Shot can rescue the synapse reduction phenotype in tau mutant neurons.
source: Finally, we performed cross-rescue experiments by expressing a shot transgene in tauMR22 mutant neurons and a tau transgene in shot3 mutant neurons. In both cases, Syt staining revealed a rescue of the synapse reduction phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-rescue experiments showing that Shot expression rescues tau mutant phenotypes.

claim: Tau can rescue the synapse reduction phenotype in shot mutant neurons.
source: Finally, we performed cross-rescue experiments by expressing a shot transgene in tauMR22 mutant neurons and a tau transgene in shot3 mutant neurons. In both cases, Syt staining revealed a rescue of the synapse reduction phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-rescue experiments showing that Tau expression rescues shot mutant phenotypes.

claim: Shot and Tau functionally overlap rather than act hierarchically in the same pathway.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that Shot and Tau functionally overlap, rather than act hierarchically in the same pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic interaction and cross-rescue experiments.

claim: In shot-tau mutant embryos at stage 16, Syt levels at NMJs are reduced to 48%.
source: In shot-tau mutant embryos, Syt levels at NMJs were reduced to 48%, whereas shot mutant embryos showed a milder reduction to 71%, and tau mutant embryos no detectable effect (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring Syt levels at NMJs in mutant embryos.

claim: In shot mutant embryos at stage 16, Syt levels at NMJs are reduced to 71%.
source: In shot-tau mutant embryos, Syt levels at NMJs were reduced to 48%, whereas shot mutant embryos showed a milder reduction to 71%, and tau mutant embryos no detectable effect (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring Syt levels at NMJs in mutant embryos.

claim: Tau mutant embryos at stage 16 show no detectable effect on Syt levels at NMJs.
source: In shot-tau mutant embryos, Syt levels at NMJs were reduced to 48%, whereas shot mutant embryos showed a milder reduction to 71%, and tau mutant embryos no detectable effect (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring Syt levels at NMJs in mutant embryos.

claim: Tau is required for synapse formation in culture and in vivo.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that Tau is required for the formation of synapses in culture and in vivo and that Tau and Shot functionally overlap in this context.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from both cultured neurons and in vivo embryonic studies.

claim: Aged Tau knock-out mice develop a reduction of synaptic proteins from the hippocampus.
source: Notably, the synaptic function of Tau described here for Drosophila might be conserved in higher animals or humans, since also aged Tau knock-out mice develop a reduction of synaptic proteins from the hippocampus (Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on Tau knock-out mice.

claim: Combined knock-down of tau and shot in primary neurons at 3 DIV and 18 DIV causes no reduction in the number of Syt-labelled presynaptic sites compared to wildtype controls.
source: We first used this approach in cultured primary neurons, where combined knock-down of tau and shot caused no reduction in the number of Syt-labelled presynaptic sites at 3 and 18 DIV as compared to wildtype controls (Figure 3A–B), indicating normal synapse development.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing synapse numbers at different time points.

claim: Combined knock-down of tau and shot in primary neurons at 26 DIV causes Syt puncta to be reduced to 41%.
source: However, at 26 DIV, Syt puncta in knock-down neurons were reduced to 41% (Figure 3A–B), which was comparable to the shot-tau double-mutant phenotype at 2 DIV (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring synapse numbers at 26 DIV.

claim: At 3, 18 and 26 DIV, tau and shot knock-down neurons show no measurable changes in axonal length or branch number compared to control neurons.
source: At all time points (i.e. 3, 18 and 26 DIV), there were no measurable changes in axonal length nor in branch number when compared to control neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) clearly indicating that the strong reduction in Syt positive synapses in 26 DIV knock-down neurons was not a secondary effect of morphological changes such as in number of branches and axonal length (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring axonal morphology at different time points.

claim: In aged dorsal cluster neurons (24-29 days), combined knock-down of shot and tau causes the number of Syt-GFP labelled synapses to decrease to 34% when normalized to young flies.
source: We found that the number of Syt-GFP labelled synapses in DC neurons decreased to 34% in aged specimens expressing both shotRNAi and tauRNAi when normalised to young flies of the same genotype (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing synapse numbers in young versus aged flies.

claim: In control flies, the number of Syt-GFP labelled synapses in DC neurons does not decrease with age.
source: This age-dependent decrease in synapse numbers did not occur in control flies (Figure 3C–D), and single knock-down of either shot or tau only showed a non-significant tendency to lose synapses over time (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing synapse numbers in young versus aged control flies.

claim: Single knock-down of either shot or tau shows only a non-significant tendency to lose synapses over time in DC neurons.
source: This age-dependent decrease in synapse numbers did not occur in control flies (Figure 3C–D), and single knock-down of either shot or tau only showed a non-significant tendency to lose synapses over time (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing synapse numbers in young versus aged flies with single knock-downs.

claim: Aged double knock-down DC neurons have no reduction in the number of axonal branches.
source: Notably, aged double knock-down DC neurons had no reduction in the number of axonal branches (as assessed with the myr-tdTomato membrane marker; Figure 3E–F), indicating that also in vivo precocious synapse decay was not due to axonal loss.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring axonal branches in aged flies.

claim: Tau and Shot are required for synapse development during early stages and for synapse maintenance in ageing neurons.
source: From our studies in culture, in embryos and in the adult brain, we conclude that Tau and Shot are required for synapse development during early stages, and for synapse maintenance in ageing neurons, where their combined deficiency causes precocious synapse loss.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from multiple experimental systems (culture, embryos, adult brain).

claim: At 8 hours in vitro, shot-tau double mutant neurons display a strong decrease in synaptic proteins in growth cones and axons.
source: Already at this early stage, shot-tau double mutant neurons display a strong decrease in synaptic proteins in growth cones and axons (Figure 4A–B), indicating potential intracellular transport defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring synaptic protein levels in early neurons.

claim: In shot-tau mutant neurons at 8 HIV, the percentages of anterograde and retrograde displacements of Syt-GFP containing vesicles are not affected.
source: In shot-tau mutant neurons, the percentages of anterograde and retrograde displacements and retrograde velocities of Syt-GFP containing vesicles were not affected and anterograde velocities were only slightly increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data analyzing vesicle transport dynamics.

claim: In shot-tau mutant neurons at 8 HIV, retrograde velocities of Syt-GFP containing vesicles are not affected.
source: In shot-tau mutant neurons, the percentages of anterograde and retrograde displacements and retrograde velocities of Syt-GFP containing vesicles were not affected and anterograde velocities were only slightly increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data analyzing vesicle transport dynamics.

claim: In shot-tau mutant neurons at 8 HIV, anterograde velocities of Syt-GFP containing vesicles are only slightly increased.
source: In shot-tau mutant neurons, the percentages of anterograde and retrograde displacements and retrograde velocities of Syt-GFP containing vesicles were not affected and anterograde velocities were only slightly increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data analyzing vesicle transport dynamics.

claim: In shot-tau mutant neurons at 8 HIV, the number of Syt vesicles within the axon shows a sharp decrease to ~40% compared to controls.
source: In contrast, the number of Syt vesicles within the axon showed a sharp decrease to ~40% in shot-tau mutant neurons when compared to controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data quantifying vesicle numbers in axons.

claim: In shot-tau mutant neurons at 8 HIV, the number of somatic Syt-GFP puncta is increased to ~159%.
source: Notably, this decrease in axonal vesicles is accompanied by an increase in the number of somatic Syt-GFP puncta to ~159% (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data quantifying vesicle numbers in somata.

claim: Endogenous Syt is increased in somata of shot-tau mutant neurons, both in culture and in vivo.
source: Similarly, endogenous Syt was increased in somata of shot-tau mutant neurons, both in culture and in in vivo (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring endogenous Syt levels in somata.

claim: The phenotypes in shot-tau mutant neurons suggest aberrant intracellular trafficking of Syt-containing vesicles, potentially due to a road block in the soma.
source: These phenotypes in shot-tau mutant neurons suggested aberrant intracellular trafficking of Syt-containing vesicles, potentially due to a road block in the soma.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of vesicle distribution.

claim: Unc-104 is the predominant motor driving axonal transport of synaptic proteins in Drosophila.
source: Type 3 kinesins are the predominant motors driving axonal transport of synaptic proteins (Hirokawa et al., 2010). This is also the case for the Drosophila homologue Unc-104 (also called Imac) (Pack-Chung et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on kinesin-3 motors.

claim: unc-104170 null mutant primary neurons at 2 DIV have a vast reduction of Syt-stained synapses.
source: We found that unc-104170 null mutant primary neurons at 2 DIV have a vast reduction of Syt-stained synapses (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring synapse numbers in unc-104 mutant neurons.

claim: The unc-104 mutant phenotype is strikingly similar to the shot-tau mutant phenotype.
source: This phenotype is strikingly similar to the one observed in shot-tau mutant neurons, and suggested that Shot-Tau might regulate Unc-104 function.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of phenotypes between different mutants.

claim: Primary neurons triple-heterozygous for shot3 tauMR22 unc104imac170 mutations display significant reduction in the number of Syt-stained synapses compared to heterozygous condition of the unc-104 or shot-tau mutant alleles alone.
source: We found that primary neurons stained for Syt at 2 DIV and heterozygous for all of the three genes (shot-/+ unc-104-/+ tau-/+) displayed significant reduction in the number of Syt-stained synapses when compared to heterozygous condition of the unc-104 or shot-tau mutant alleles alone (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction studies showing synapse reduction in triple heterozygous mutants.

claim: Triple-heterozygous mutant embryos at late stage 16 display reduced Syt staining at neuromuscular terminals but increased staining in the cell bodies of CNS and sensory neurons.
source: Also triple-heterozygous mutant embryos at late stage 16 displayed reduced Syt staining at neuromuscular terminals, but increased staining in the cell bodies of CNS and sensory neurons (Figure 5C; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for a schematic drawing of the embryonic NMJ and CNS).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring Syt distribution in embryos.

claim: unc-104170 mutant, shot-tau mutant, and triple-heterozygous mutant neurons all show similar phenotypes, both in culture and in vivo, suggesting a functional link between these three proteins.
source: Therefore, unc-104170 mutant, shot-tau mutant, and triple-heterozygous mutant neurons all show similar phenotypes, both in culture and in vivo, suggesting a functional link between these three proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparison of phenotypes across different mutants.

claim: Drosophila Unc-104 is distally enriched in the axons of primary neurons at 2 DIV.
source: Type 3 kinesins are anterograde motor proteins that move towards axon tips in mouse neurons (Niwa et al., 2013), and we also find Drosophila Unc-104 to be distally enriched in the axons of primary neurons at 2 DIV and in embryonic motorneurons in vivo (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Unc-104 localization in axons.

claim: Drosophila Unc-104 is distally enriched in embryonic motorneurons in vivo.
source: Type 3 kinesins are anterograde motor proteins that move towards axon tips in mouse neurons (Niwa et al., 2013), and we also find Drosophila Unc-104 to be distally enriched in the axons of primary neurons at 2 DIV and in embryonic motorneurons in vivo (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Unc-104 localization in embryonic neurons.

claim: In mouse neurons, distal localization of kinesin-3 is suppressed when blocking kinesin-3 mobility.
source: In mouse, this distal localisation was shown to be suppressed when blocking kinesin-3 mobility (Niwa et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on kinesin-3 in mouse neurons.

claim: In shot-tau mutant neurons in culture and in vivo, Unc-104 localisation in distal axons is reduced whereas levels in the somata are increased.
source: Also in shot-tau mutant neurons in culture and in vivo, Unc-104 localisation in distal axons is reduced whereas levels in the somata are increased (Figure 5D–E), suggesting that insufficient amounts of Unc-104 move from the somata into axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring Unc-104 distribution in mutant neurons.

claim: Over-expression of Unc-104 fully restores synapse numbers in shot-tau mutant neurons at 2 DIV.
source: To test whether diminished Unc-104 levels in axons are the cause for the synaptic defects in shot-tau mutant conditions, we over-expressed Unc-104, which fully restored synapse numbers in shot-tau mutant neurons at 2 DIV (Figures 5B versus 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that Unc-104 overexpression restores synapse numbers.

claim: Unc-104 over-expression in shot-tau mutant neurons rescues synapses in neurons with significantly less axonal branches.
source: Notably, Unc-104 over-expression in shot-tau mutant neurons achieved this rescue of synapses in neurons with significantly less axonal branches (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F), clearly demonstrating that both features are regulated independently of each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of synapses without rescue of branch numbers.

claim: Co-expression of Unc-104 together with shotRNAi and tauRNAi rescues age-dependent synapse reduction in DC neurons.
source: When Unc-104 was co-expressed, synapse reduction was clearly rescued (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of age-dependent synapse loss.

claim: Shot localises along microtubules.
source: Shot localises along microtubules, and shot mutant neurons treated with the microtubule-destabilising drug nocodazole display unusual gaps in their axonal microtubule bundles (Figure 6B–C) (Alves-Silva et al., 2012; Sanchez-Soriano et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to published work.

claim: Shot mutant neurons treated with nocodazole display unusual gaps in their axonal microtubule bundles.
source: Shot localises along microtubules, and shot mutant neurons treated with the microtubule-destabilising drug nocodazole display unusual gaps in their axonal microtubule bundles (Figure 6B–C) (Alves-Silva et al., 2012; Sanchez-Soriano et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing microtubule gaps upon nocodazole treatment.

claim: Tau localises along microtubules.
source: Tau also localises along microtubules (Figure 6A, Video 1), and tauMR22 mutant neurons likewise displayed axonal microtubule gaps upon nocodazole treatment which could be rescued with targeted expression of Tau (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Tau localization along microtubules.

claim: tauMR22 mutant neurons display axonal microtubule gaps upon nocodazole treatment.
source: Tau also localises along microtubules (Figure 6A, Video 1), and tauMR22 mutant neurons likewise displayed axonal microtubule gaps upon nocodazole treatment which could be rescued with targeted expression of Tau (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing microtubule gaps in tau mutant neurons upon nocodazole treatment.

claim: Targeted expression of Tau rescues axonal microtubule gaps in tauMR22 mutant neurons treated with nocodazole.
source: Tau also localises along microtubules (Figure 6A, Video 1), and tauMR22 mutant neurons likewise displayed axonal microtubule gaps upon nocodazole treatment which could be rescued with targeted expression of Tau (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that Tau expression prevents microtubule gaps.

claim: Both shot and tau mutant neurons treated with nocodazole display on average one gap per axon.
source: Both, shot and tau mutant neurons treated with nocodazole displayed on average one gap per axon.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying microtubule gaps.

claim: Shot-tau mutant neurons treated with nocodazole display on average ~3 gaps per axon.
source: This number is significantly increased to ~3 gaps in shot-tau mutant neurons (Figure 6B–C), demonstrating that Tau and Shot share a common function in microtubule stabilisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying microtubule gaps in double mutants.

claim: Tau and Shot share a common function in microtubule stabilisation.
source: This number is significantly increased to ~3 gaps in shot-tau mutant neurons (Figure 6B–C), demonstrating that Tau and Shot share a common function in microtubule stabilisation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing additive effects in double mutants.

claim: Treatment of shot-tau mutant embryos with epothilone B significantly rescues Syt levels at motoraxonal endings.
source: To test whether their roles in microtubule stabilisation and synapse regulation are linked, we treated shot-tau mutant embryos at early stage 16 for 3 hr with the microtubule-stabilising drug epothilone B (Goodin et al., 2004). We found a significant rescue of Syt levels at motoraxonal endings, which was not observed in vehicle-treated controls (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of Syt levels with epothilone B treatment.

claim: A decrease in microtubule stability is a likely cause for defective transport of synaptic proteins in shot-tau mutant neurons.
source: Therefore, a decrease in microtubule stability is a likely cause for defective transport of synaptic proteins in shot-tau mutant neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from drug rescue experiments.

claim: In wild type embryos at stage 16, high accumulations of JNK-P are found at motoraxon tips and low levels in the somata of CNS and sensory neurons.
source: In wild type embryos at stage 16, we found high accumulations of JNK-P at motoraxon tips and low levels in the somata of CNS and sensory neurons (Figures 6F and 7A), i.e. a localisation pattern similar to that of synaptic proteins and Unc-104 (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing JNK-P distribution in wildtype embryos.

claim: In single tauMR22 or shot3 mutant embryos, JNK-P shows higher levels in neuronal somata and lower levels at the tips of motoraxons.
source: This distribution was altered in single tauMR22 or shot3 mutant embryos, showing higher levels of JNK-P in neuronal somata and lower levels at the tips of motoraxons (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing altered JNK-P distribution in single mutants.

claim: The altered JNK-P pattern is intensified in shot-tau double mutant neurons.
source: This altered pattern was intensified in shot-tau double mutant neurons (Figure 7A) and clearly reminiscent of the redistribution patterns observed with synaptic proteins and Unc-104 in these neurons (Figures 4E and 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing JNK-P distribution in double mutants.

claim: Application of nocodazole to early stage 16 wildtype embryos reproduces the changes in the pattern of JNK activation observed in shot-tau mutants.
source: Notably, these changes in the pattern of JNK activation were reproduced when inducing microtubule stress by applying nocodazole to early stage 16 wildtype embryos (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that nocodazole treatment mimics the mutant phenotype.

claim: Treatment of shot-tau mutant neurons with epothilone B increases the localisation of JNK-P at axonal tips and reduces the aberrant localisation in somata.
source: Complementary to this finding, treatment of shot-tau mutant neurons with the microtubule stabilising drug epothilone B, increased the localisation of JNK-P at axonal tips and reduced the aberrant localisation in somata (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of JNK-P distribution with epothilone B treatment.

claim: Shot-tau mediated microtubule destabilisation or stress triggers abnormal JNK activity patterns with upregulation in somata and downregulation at axon tips.
source: These data suggested a cascade of events where shot-tau mediated microtubule destabilisation or stress triggers abnormal JNK activation in somata which, in turn, causes a somatic block of Unc-104 mediated synaptic transport.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of JNK-P distribution and drug treatments.

claim: Aberrant JNK activation leads to a somatic roadblock for kinesin-3 mediated transport, inhibiting the delivery of synaptic proteins and causing synapse loss.
source: These data suggested a cascade of events where shot-tau mediated microtubule destabilisation or stress triggers abnormal JNK activation in somata which, in turn, causes a somatic block of Unc-104 mediated synaptic transport.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of protein distributions and genetic interactions.

claim: JNK-P, Unc-104 and synaptic proteins show a striking correlation by concentrating unanimously at axon tips in wildtype, but in somata in shot-tau mutant neurons.
source: In strong support of this hypothesis, the three key players of this cascade, JNK-P, Unc-104 and synaptic proteins, show a striking correlation by concentrating unanimously at axon tips in wildtype, but in somata in shot-tau mutant neurons (Figures 4E, 5E and 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlated distributions of multiple proteins.

claim: Expression of constitutively active HepAC in late stage 16 embryos triggers an accumulation of Unc-104 and Syt in somata and a decrease of both proteins at axon tips.
source: To prove that JNK acts downstream of shot-tau to regulate Unc-104, we first expressed a constitutively active variant of the MAPKK Hemipterous (HepAC), a known activator of the JNK pathway (Glise et al., 1995). In late stage 16 embryos, indiscriminate JNK activation through HepAC triggered an accumulation of Unc-104 and Syt in somata and a decrease of both proteins at axon tips (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of JNK activation on protein distribution.

claim: HepAC expression in primary mature neurons at 2 DIV causes a reduction in the number of synapses to 43%.
source: Also in primary mature neurons at 2 DIV, HepAC caused a reduction in the number of synapses to 43% (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring synapse numbers upon HepAC expression.

claim: HepAC expression mimics the defects observed in shot-tau mutant neurons.
source: Therefore, HepAC expression mimicked the defects observed in shot-tau mutant neurons, consistent with a model where aberrant JNK pathway activation upon Shot-Tau loss causes the somatic block of Unc-104-dependent synaptic transport.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of phenotypes between HepAC expression and shot-tau mutants.

claim: The wnd2 mutation fully rescues the synaptic defects in tauMR22 mutant primary neurons at 2 DIV.
source: To downregulate the JNK pathway, we used loss-of-function of the JNK activating kinase Wallenda/DLK (wnd2) (Valakh et al., 2013) and overexpression of the JNK inhibiting phosphatase Puckered (Puc) (Martin-Blanco et al., 1998). When combined with the tauMR22 mutation, both genetic tools for JNK downregulation fully rescued the synaptic defects in primary neurons at 2 DIV (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that JNK downregulation rescues synaptic defects.

claim: Overexpression of Puc fully rescues the synaptic defects in tauMR22 mutant primary neurons at 2 DIV.
source: To downregulate the JNK pathway, we used loss-of-function of the JNK activating kinase Wallenda/DLK (wnd2) (Valakh et al., 2013) and overexpression of the JNK inhibiting phosphatase Puckered (Puc) (Martin-Blanco et al., 1998). When combined with the tauMR22 mutation, both genetic tools for JNK downregulation fully rescued the synaptic defects in primary neurons at 2 DIV (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that JNK downregulation rescues synaptic defects.

claim: The wnd2 mutation fully rescues synapse reduction in shot-tau double mutant neurons at 2 DIV.
source: Even more, wnd2 fully rescued synapse reduction in shot-tau double mutant neurons at 2 DIV (Figure 8A–B), and Syt levels at NMJs of shot-tau mutant embryos in vivo (Figure 8C–D versus Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that wnd2 rescues synaptic defects in double mutants.

claim: The wnd2 mutation rescues Syt levels at NMJs of shot-tau mutant embryos in vivo.
source: Even more, wnd2 fully rescued synapse reduction in shot-tau double mutant neurons at 2 DIV (Figure 8A–B), and Syt levels at NMJs of shot-tau mutant embryos in vivo (Figure 8C–D versus Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that wnd2 rescues Syt levels at NMJs.

claim: The wnd2 mutation restores correct localisation of Unc-104 in shot-tau double mutant neurons at 2 DIV.
source: Accordingly, wnd2 restored correct localisation of Unc-104 in shot-tau double mutant neurons at 2 DIV (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and in shot-tau mutant embryos in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B versus Figure 5D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that wnd2 rescues Unc-104 localization.

claim: The wnd2 mutation restores correct localisation of Unc-104 in shot-tau mutant embryos in vivo.
source: Accordingly, wnd2 restored correct localisation of Unc-104 in shot-tau double mutant neurons at 2 DIV (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and in shot-tau mutant embryos in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B versus Figure 5D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that wnd2 rescues Unc-104 localization in vivo.

claim: The kay2 mutation fails to rescue the synaptic phenotypes of tauMR22 in primary neurons.
source: For this, we used a well established LOF mutant allele of the kayak/c-fos gene (kay2) which removes one constituent of the AP1 heterodimer and mimics various known JNK mutant phenotypes (Ciapponi and Bohmann, 2002). Unlike wnd2 or Puc overexpression, the kay2 mutation failed to rescue the synaptic phenotypes of tauMR22 in primary neurons (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that kay2 does not rescue synaptic defects.

claim: The JNK pathway inhibits synaptic transport by acting independently of AP1 dependent transcription.
source: This strongly suggests that the JNK pathway inhibits synaptic transport by acting independently of AP1 dependent transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the failure of kay2 to rescue synaptic defects.

claim: The JNK pathway is both required and sufficient to mediate between Shot-Tau loss and their downstream synaptic phenotypes in developing neurons by causing a transport roadblock.
source: In conclusion, the JNK pathway is both required and sufficient to mediate between Shot-Tau loss and their downstream synaptic phenotypes in developing neurons by causing a transport roadblock, and this likely occurs through phosphorylating cytoplasmic targets in the soma.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies.

claim: Co-expression of bskDN rescues the synapse reduction phenotype in aged DC neurons with shot and tau knock-down.
source: We found that co-expression of bskDN was able to rescue the synapse reduction phenotype (Figure 8E,F), thus confirming JNK as a mediator between the effects of shot-tau and precocious synapse decay also in ageing neurons (summarised in Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that JNK inhibition rescues age-dependent synapse loss.

claim: JNK is a mediator between the effects of shot-tau and precocious synapse decay in ageing neurons.
source: We found that co-expression of bskDN was able to rescue the synapse reduction phenotype (Figure 8E,F), thus confirming JNK as a mediator between the effects of shot-tau and precocious synapse decay also in ageing neurons (summarised in Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from rescue experiments in aged neurons.

claim: Microdeletions in the region of MAPT (the human tau gene) cause intellectual disability.
source: For example, microdeletions in the region of MAPT (the human tau gene) cause intellectual disability (Sapir et al., 2012), and Tau's synapse-promoting roles m﻿ay well contribute to this pathology.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on MAPT deletions.

claim: Various tauopathies are characterised by precocious pathological loss of synapses.
source: Furthermore, various tauopathies are characterised by precocious pathological loss of synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about tauopathies.

claim: Loss of tau could lead to defective synapse maintenance and eventually synapse loss.
source: Our data suggest that loss of tau could lead to defective synapse maintenance and eventually synapse loss.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results showing synapse loss in tau-deficient conditions.

claim: A prominent group of dementias which lacks distinctive histopathology (DLDH) are characterised by the loss of Tau.
source: For example, a prominent group of dementias which lacks distinctive histopathology (DLDH) are characterised by the loss of Tau (Zhukareva et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on DLDH.

claim: Tauopathies including Alzheimer disease typically involve hyper-phosphorylation and aggregate formation of Tau.
source: Further tauopathies including Alzheimer disease, typically involve hyper-phosphorylation and aggregate formation of Tau (Hernández and Avila, 2007; Williams, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on tauopathies.

claim: Hyper-phosphorylation of tau causes a loss-of-function condition by depleting Tau from microtubules.
source: Secondly, hyper-phosphorylation of tau causes a loss-of-function condition by depleting Tau from microtubules.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about tau phosphorylation.

claim: Tau knock-out mouse models mostly failed to show significant phenotypes.
source: However, since Tau knock-out mouse models mostly failed to show significant phenotypes and the neuronal functions of endogenous tau remain little understood, the pathological importance of Tau loss from microtubules has been marginalised (Morris et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on tau knock-out mice.

claim: Loss of Tau from microtubules could contribute to neurodegenerative pathology.
source: Our results now re-emphasise the notion that loss of Tau from microtubules could contribute to neurodegenerative pathology and deliver mechanistic explanations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results showing phenotypes upon tau loss.

claim: Spectraplakins are MAPs which functionally overlap with Tau.
source: Our discovery that spectraplakins are MAPs which functionally overlap with Tau, opens up new experimental avenues for Tau studies.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing functional overlap between Shot and Tau.

claim: Spectraplakins have been linked to the degeneration of sensory and autonomous neurons.
source: So far, spectraplakins have been linked to the degeneration of sensory and autonomous neurons (Edvardson et al., 2012; Ferrier et al., 2013), and it remains to be elucidated whether they may have similar roles also in the brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on spectraplakins.

claim: The loss of Tau and/or Shot inhibits kinesin-3 mediated transport leading to accumulation of synaptic proteins in the soma of neurons.
source: The loss of Tau and/or Shot inhibits kinesin-3 mediated transport leading to accumulation of synaptic proteins in the soma of neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing protein accumulation in somata.

claim: A road-block mechanism suppresses the initiation of axonal transport in somata of Shot-Tau depleted neurons, which is caused indirectly through microtubule stress and mediated by JNK.
source: We propose a road-block mechanism suppressing the initiation of axonal transport in somata of Shot-Tau depleted neurons, which is caused indirectly through microtubule stress and mediated by JNK (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including drug treatments and genetic manipulations.

claim: Axonal transport defects and cognitive deficits of PS19Tg mice and various other mouse and fly tauopathy models were shown to be rescued by microtubule-stabilising drugs.
source: Similarly, axonal transport defects and cognitive deficits of PS19Tg mice (expressing the P301S mutant form of human tau) and various other mouse and fly tauopathy models were shown to be rescued by microtubule-stabilising drugs (Gozes, 2011; Quraishe et al., 2013; Shemesh and Spira, 2011; Zhang et al., 2012), suggesting that the mechanisms we described may be conserved and relevant to disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on tauopathy models.

claim: The somatic road-block is a novel mechanism through which the loss of Tau can interfere with the transport of synaptic proteins.
source: The somatic road-block is a novel mechanism through which the loss of Tau can interfere with the transport of synaptic proteins and provides potential explanations also for somatic accumulations of postsynaptic proteins such as PSD-95, AMPA and NMDA receptors observed in mouse tauopathy models (Hoover et al., 2010; Shao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results and comparison with published findings.

claim: Somatic accumulations of postsynaptic proteins such as PSD-95, AMPA and NMDA receptors are observed in mouse tauopathy models.
source: The somatic road-block is a novel mechanism through which the loss of Tau can interfere with the transport of synaptic proteins and provides potential explanations also for somatic accumulations of postsynaptic proteins such as PSD-95, AMPA and NMDA receptors observed in mouse tauopathy models (Hoover et al., 2010; Shao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on mouse tauopathy models.

claim: A likely mechanism causing a roadblock in intracellular transport could be the direct inactivation of Unc-104 or its associated adaptor proteins through JNK or other kinases within its pathway.
source: A likely mechanism causing a roadblock in intracellular transport could be the direct inactivation of Unc-104 or its associated adaptor proteins, for example through JNK or other kinases within its pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential molecular mechanisms.

claim: Kinesin-1 and its adaptor Jip are directly phosphorylated by JNK leading to transport inhibition.
source: This mode of regulation has a clear precedent in kinesin-1 and its adaptor Jip which are directly phosphorylated by JNK leading to transport inhibition (Stagi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on kinesin-1 regulation.

claim: In mouse, microtubule stress leads to somatic activation of the JNK pathway.
source: Also in mouse, microtubule stress leads to somatic activation of the JNK pathway, suggesting this mechanism is likely to be conserved with vertebrates (Valakh et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on JNK activation in mouse.

claim: JNK is emerging as a central player in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The JNK pathway is emerging as a central player in neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about JNK in neurodegeneration.

claim: JNK activation is prompted by various neurodegeneration risk factors including oxidative stress, inflammation, and ageing.
source: Its activation is prompted by various neurodegeneration risk factors including oxidative stress, inflammation, and ageing (Lotharius et al., 2005; Valakh et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on JNK activation.

claim: JNK is activated in AD patients.
source: Furthermore, JNK is activated in AD patients (Coffey, 2014) and in several AD models where it triggers progression of the pathology (Sclip et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on JNK in AD.

claim: In several AD models, JNK triggers progression of the pathology.
source: Furthermore, JNK is activated in AD patients (Coffey, 2014) and in several AD models where it triggers progression of the pathology (Sclip et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on JNK in AD models.

claim: The new link between Tau/spectraplakins, JNK and synapses is likely to provide mechanistic explanations for synaptic pathology observed in AD and other tauopathies.
source: The new link between Tau/spectraplakins, JNK and synapses we propose here, is therefore likely to provide mechanistic explanations for synaptic pathology observed in AD and other tauopathies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results and their potential relevance to disease.

claim: Tau detachment from microtubules can be an important aspect contributing to the pathology of tauopathies in parallel to roles of hyper-phosphorylated Tau in the cytoplasm.
source: Our findings emphasise that Tau detachment from microtubules can be an important aspect contributing to the pathology of tauopathies in parallel to roles of hyper-phosphorylated Tau in the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results showing phenotypes upon tau loss.

claim: Synaptic decay, axonal transport and alterations in the JNK pathway are emerging as central players in a wider range of adult-onset neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Synaptic decay, axonal transport and alterations in the JNK pathway are emerging as central players in a wider range of adult-onset neurodegenerative diseases, and here we have aligned these factors into a concrete mechanistic cascade.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Precocious loss of synapses is observed in late onset neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD).
source: Precocious loss of synapses is observed in late onset neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD), likely contributing to the cognitive decline and neuronal decay observed in patients (Pooler et al., 2014; Saxena and Caroni, 2007; Serrano-Pozo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on synapse loss in neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: The development of synapses and their maintenance during ageing is dependent on sustained transport of synaptic proteins from the distant soma, driven by motor proteins which trail along the bundles of microtubules in axons and dendrites.
source: The development of synapses and their maintenance during ageing is dependent on sustained transport of synaptic proteins from the distant soma, driven by motor proteins which trail along the bundles of microtubules in axons and dendrites (Goldstein et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on axonal transport.

claim: Microtubules are regulated by microtubule binding proteins which are in a key position to regulate synapse formation and maintenance.
source: Microtubules are regulated by microtubule binding proteins which are therefore in a key position to regulate synapse formation and maintenance (Prokop, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on microtubule binding proteins.

claim: Tau is a microtubule associated protein (MAP) discovered in the mid-seventies.
source: Tau is a microtubule associated protein (MAP) discovered in the mid-seventies (Weingarten et al., 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the original discovery of Tau.

claim: Reduction in Tau levels has been linked to intellectual disability.
source: Reduction in Tau levels has been linked to intellectual disability (Sapir et al., 2012) and a class of brain disorders termed 'dementias which lack distinctive histopathology' (DLDH) (Zhukareva et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on Tau reduction and intellectual disability.

claim: Reduction in Tau levels has been linked to a class of brain disorders termed 'dementias which lack distinctive histopathology' (DLDH).
source: Reduction in Tau levels has been linked to intellectual disability (Sapir et al., 2012) and a class of brain disorders termed 'dementias which lack distinctive histopathology' (DLDH) (Zhukareva et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on DLDH.

claim: Tau detachment from MTs is linked to prominent neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Frontotemporal Dementia and some forms of Parkinson's disease.
source: Tau detachment from MTs is linked to prominent neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Frontotemporal Dementia and some forms of Parkinson's disease (Kovacs, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on tau-related diseases.

claim: In vitro, Tau has the ability to regulate microtubule properties including stability, cross-linkage and polymerisation.
source: In vitro, Tau has the ability to regulate microtubule properties including stability, cross-linkage and polymerisation (Morris et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on Tau's in vitro properties.

claim: The physiological roles of Tau are still not understood and highly debated.
source: Through such functions, Tau would be expected to regulate multiple aspects of neuronal cell biology, but its physiological roles are still not understood and highly debated (Morris et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work discussing Tau's physiological roles.

claim: Other MAPs are proposed to mask physiological roles of Tau through functional redundancy.
source: This might partly be due to experimental challenges posed by functional redundancy, where other MAPs are proposed to mask physiological roles of Tau (Ma et al., 2014; Takei et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on functional redundancy of MAPs.

claim: Drosophila neurons provide access to powerful genetics and are readily established for research on the neuronal cytoskeleton, neuronal transport and synapses.
source: As is ideal for studies of Tau, Drosophila neurons provide access to powerful genetics, they are readily established for research on the neuronal cytoskeleton (Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2010), on neuronal transport (Schwarz, 2013) and on synapses (Prokop and Meinertzhagen, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on Drosophila neurons.

claim: Concepts and mechanisms gained from work in flies are often well conserved in higher organisms.
source: Importantly, concepts and mechanisms gained from work in flies are often well conserved in higher organisms (Bellen et al., 2010; Jaiswal et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on conservation of mechanisms from flies to higher organisms.

claim: The spectraplakin Short Stop (Shot) could display potential functional overlap with Tau during microtubule stabilisation.
source: Work in Drosophila suggested that the spectraplakin Short Stop (Shot), a large actin-MT linker molecules and potent regulators of microtubules, could display potential functional overlap with Tau during microtubule stabilisation (Alves-Silva et al., 2012; Prokop, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work suggesting functional overlap.

claim: The mammalian spectraplakin Dystonin is linked to a neurodegenerative disease (type VI hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathy).
source: This hypothesis is attractive because the well-conserved mammalian spectraplakin Dystonin is already linked to a neurodegenerative disease (type VI hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathy; OMIM #614653;) (Ferrier et al., 2013), and its paralogue ACF7/MACF1 plays important roles during brain development (Goryunov et al., 2010; Ka and Kim, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on Dystonin and disease.

claim: ACF7/MACF1 plays important roles during brain development.
source: This hypothesis is attractive because the well-conserved mammalian spectraplakin Dystonin is already linked to a neurodegenerative disease (type VI hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathy; OMIM #614653;) (Ferrier et al., 2013), and its paralogue ACF7/MACF1 plays important roles during brain development (Goryunov et al., 2010; Ka and Kim, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on ACF7/MACF1.

claim: ACF7 continues to be expressed in the brain.
source: Since ACF7 continues to be expressed in the brain, it is tempting to speculate that it might be required for neuronal maintenance (Bernier et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on ACF7 expression.

claim: Primary fly neurons at 2 DIV display functional presynaptic sites.
source: Already 8 hr in vitro (HIV), these neurons show transport of synaptic material in the growing axon (Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2010) and after 2 days in vitro (DIV), they display functional presynaptic sites (Küppers-Munther et al., 2004; Küppers et al., 2003) that can be reliably stained with antibodies against presynaptic proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on primary fly neurons.

claim: Primary fly neurons at 2 DIV contain dense bars and synaptic vesicle accumulations which undergo excitation-dependent uptake and release.
source: They contain dense bars and synaptic vesicle accumulations which undergo excitation-dependent uptake and release (Küppers-Munther et al., 2004; Küppers et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on synaptic vesicle dynamics in primary fly neurons.

claim: The Df(3R)tauMR22 mutation (tauMR22) is an embryonic lethal chromosome deletion that uncovers most of the Drosophila tau gene and is a true null allele.
source: The Df(3R)tauMR22 mutation (tauMR22) is an embryonic lethal chromosome deletion that uncovers most of the Drosophila tau gene and is a true null allele (Bolkan and Kretzschmar, 2014; Doerflinger et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work characterizing the tauMR22 mutation.

claim: At embryonic stage 16, Syt is already confined to nascent synaptic terminals at neuromuscular junctions.
source: Since shot3 and tauMR22 animals are late embryonic lethal, we analysed them at late embryonic stage 16, when Syt is already confined to nascent synaptic terminals, as can be reliably imaged at neuromuscular junctions (NMJs; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for a schematic drawing of the embryonic NMJ) (Littleton et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on Syt localization at embryonic NMJs.

claim: In Drosophila primary neurons, transport of endogenous synaptic proteins already starts at 8 hr in vitro (HIV) when synaptic proteins appear as dotted patterns along axons and in growth cones.
source: In Drosophila primary neurons, transport of endogenous synaptic proteins already starts at 8 hr in vitro (HIV) when synaptic proteins appear as dotted patterns along axons and in growth cones (Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2010) (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on synaptic protein transport.

claim: In rat hippocampal neurons, synaptic proteins appear as dotted patterns along axons and in growth cones similar to Drosophila neurons.
source: This is similar in rat hippocampal neurons (Bonanomi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on rat hippocampal neurons.
